\begin{frame}{Setup}
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}\small
      \lbl{SCENES} OB3D, with reference depth and normals:
      \code{sponza}, \code{lone-monk}, \code{emerald-square}.

      \lbl{PROTOCOL} 7k iterations. Reference geometry is read by evaluation only; no training
      term uses it. Held-out split for all metrics.

      \lbl{SEED NOISE} over \code{seed\_initialization} 1--4:
      \begin{itemize}
        \item PSNR $\pm$0.04--0.13\,dB
        \item \code{abs\_rel} $\pm$0.002--0.004
        \item normal $\pm$0.1--1.2$^\circ$
      \end{itemize}
      Single-term cells are 3-seed; combination cells are single-seed.
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}\small
      \lbl{METRICS}
      \begin{itemize}
        \item \code{abs\_rel} --- mean $|d - d^{*}|/d^{*}$ over pixels where the reference has
              depth and the ray is opaque enough to have one.
        \item normal$^\circ$ --- mean angle to the reference normal, signed (a flipped normal
              scores 180$^\circ$, not 0$^\circ$).
        \item \code{n\_gain} --- \textbf{control}: normal$^\circ$ of the view-direction control
              minus normal$^\circ$ of the render. The control points every normal back along the
              view ray and uses no geometry.
        \item PSNR --- on the composited image, as validation reports it.
      \end{itemize}
      \vspace{0.3em}
      {\footnotesize\dn{$\mathbf{n\_gain < 0}$}: the normal buffer is worse than using no
      geometry at all.}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
\end{frame}

\section{Experiment 1: depth--normal consistency}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 1: depth--normal consistency}
  \pre The rendered normal and the rendered depth are produced independently and nothing ties
  them together. The depth gradient implies a surface orientation; the normal buffer need not
  agree with it.

  \expt Penalise the angle between the rendered normal and the normal implied by the local
  geometry of the rendered depth. No external data; internal consistency only. Weight 0.05,
  \code{depth\_normal\_from\_iter} lowered from 7000 to fit a 7k sweep.

  \res
  \begin{center}\scriptsize
    \input{plots/tab_dn.tex}
  \end{center}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 1: qualitative and conclusion}
  \qual \code{sponza} normals, against the reference and both reference runs.
  \begin{center}
    \quadrow
      {sponza/baseline_f4_normal_gt.png}{reference}
      {sponza/baseline_f4_normal.png}{\code{gaussian} 52.4$^\circ$}
      {sponza/trisurfel_f4_normal.png}{\code{trisurfel} 44.7$^\circ$}
      {sponza/dn05_f4_normal.png}{\code{dn 0.05} \up{25.4$^\circ$}}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.4em}
  \conc
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item Normals: beats \code{gaussian} on all three scenes by 17--27$^\circ$. Against the
          \emph{best} reference it wins on \code{sponza} (\up{$-19.3^\circ$}) and
          \code{emerald-square} (\up{$-8.1^\circ$}) and \dn{loses on \code{lone-monk}}
          (37.4$^\circ$ against \code{trisurfel}'s 35.0$^\circ$).
    \item \code{n\_gain} turns positive on \code{sponza} and \code{emerald-square}; on
          \code{lone-monk} it stays \dn{negative} ($-2.1$), as \code{gaussian}'s does.
    \item Depth: \up{$-17.0\%$} on \code{sponza}, \dn{under 1\%} on \code{lone-monk} ---
          i.e.\ nothing on the scene whose depth is worst.
    \item Cost: 0.16--0.50\,dB PSNR.
  \end{itemize}
  \textbf{Landed}, default off. The arch, masonry courses and boss are recovered from a buffer
  that was noise. But \code{lone-monk} resists it on both metrics, and had the deck compared
  only against \code{gaussian} this would have read as a clean win on all three scenes.
\end{frame}

\section{Experiment 2: depth variance along the ray}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 2: depth variance along the ray}
  \pre A ray that spreads its weight over many distances has no single surface. Penalising the
  per-ray variance of depth should make each ray commit to one.

  \expt Render per-ray $M_2$, form $\mathrm{Var} = M_2 - D^2/\mathrm{acc}$, penalise it.
  Then the scale-free form $\mathrm{Var}/\mu^2 = \mathrm{acc}\cdot M_2/D^2 - 1$, which needed no
  new buffer, kernel or backward pass. Weights 1 and 0.01.

  \res
  \begin{center}\scriptsize
    \input{plots/tab_dv.tex}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.3em}
  {\footnotesize The absolute form (earlier sweep, not in this table) gave \dn{$+6\%$}
  \code{abs\_rel} on \code{sponza} and raised the floater fraction from 0.30\% to 1.62\%. From
  \code{depth\_variance\_mechanism.py}: per-ray spread $\times0.17$ while
  \code{wrong\,|\,tight} rose \dn{$\times170$}.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 2: mechanism and conclusion}
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.54\textwidth}
      \lbl{WHY} In pairwise form,
      \[ M_2 - \tfrac{D^2}{\mathrm{acc}} = \tfrac{1}{2\,\mathrm{acc}}\textstyle\sum_{ij} w_i w_j (t_i-t_j)^2 \]
      \begin{itemize}\small
        \item Variance is zero for a Dirac at \emph{any} distance: the objective says commit,
              never where.
        \item Two-hit case is a \textbf{double well} in the near opacity, since
              $w_\mathrm{near} w_\mathrm{far}$ carries $\alpha(1-\alpha)$.
        \item The near well is \textbf{absorbing}: at $\alpha=1$ transmittance zeroes the
              gradient to everything behind, for every loss. The error is permanent.
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.44\textwidth}
      \lbl{RESCALING} Dividing by $\mu^2$ leaves both wells at exactly zero, and was first
      dismissed for that reason.
      \begin{center}\small
      \begin{tabular}{lcc}
        \toprule
        & absolute & relative \\
        \midrule
        separatrix & 0.49 & \textbf{0.82} \\
        bad basin & 51\% & \textbf{18\%} \\
        \code{sponza} & \dn{$+6\%$} & \up{$-7.9\%$} \\
        \bottomrule
      \end{tabular}
      \end{center}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
  \vspace{0.4em}
  \conc
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item \dn{Refuted as posed}: the absolute form did what it was asked --- rays six times
          tighter --- and became 170 times more likely to be confidently wrong.
    \item The relative form at 0.01 improves depth on \code{sponza} (\up{$-7.9\%$}) at no PSNR
          cost, but against the best reference it is \dn{null} on \code{emerald-square}
          ($-0.2\%$) and \dn{worse} on \code{lone-monk} ($+1.2\%$). Normals untouched.
    \item Identical minima, different behaviour: descent responds to the barrier, not the
          location of the optima.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\section{Experiment 3: pseudo-depth regression}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 3: regression against a monocular prior}
  \pre A monocular depth model carries information the scene does not. Plan: supervise it with a
  scale-invariant loss, fitting per-image scale and shift so the predictor's arbitrary affine
  gauge is not supervised.

  \expt Before training anything: measure the prior itself.
  \code{DepthAnythingV2-Base} on \code{sponza}, affine-aligned against \emph{ground truth} at
  decreasing granularity --- the most favourable alignment possible, since it uses the reference
  the loss would not have.
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.44\textwidth}
      \begin{center}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{plots/prior_alignment.pdf}\end{center}
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.54\textwidth}
      \res
      \begin{itemize}\small
        \item One affine per frame: \dn{0.0677}, against \textbf{0.0580} for the 7k model it
              would be teaching.
        \item Per 64$\times$64 patch: 0.0158. Per 16$\times$16: \up{0.0116}.
        \item Correlation with $1/z$ is $+0.978$; an affine fit reaches $R^2$ 0.956 in disparity
              against 0.821 in depth.
        \item The prior emits z-depth; this renderer's convention is Euclidean ray distance.
              Radial divergence reaches 20\% at the image corners.
      \end{itemize}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
  \conc \dn{Abandoned before training.} A globally aligned prior is worse than the model it
  would teach, and the local numbers say why: the useful structure is not in any single affine
  gauge, so scale-invariance --- the exact remedy planned --- does not recover it.
\end{frame}

\section{Experiment 4: ordinal pseudo-depth}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 4: ordinal supervision from the same prior}
  \pre Only the prior's \emph{ordering} survived the diagnostic. On pixels where the trained
  model fails \code{delta1}, the prior is closer to the reference 91\% of the time.

  \expt Read the ordering only. For a pixel pair, penalise the rendered gap only where render
  and prior disagree about which is nearer:
  \setlength{\abovedisplayskip}{2pt}\setlength{\belowdisplayskip}{2pt}
  \[
    \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{(a,b)\in\mathcal{P}}
      \mathrm{relu}\!\big(-(d_a - d_b)\cdot \mathrm{sign}(\mathrm{disp}_b - \mathrm{disp}_a)\big)
      \;/\; \text{scene extent}
  \]
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item Invariant to \emph{any} increasing transform of the prior: disposes of alignment, the
          disparity inversion and z-vs-ray-distance at once.
    \item One-sided: a correctly ordered pair contributes zero and no gradient.
    \item Pairs formed by \emph{cropping} at a random offset $\le$5\% of the image side, not
          \code{torch.roll}, which would wrap opposite edges into pairs.
  \end{itemize}
  \vspace{-0.3em}
  \res
  \begin{center}\scriptsize
    \input{plots/tab_pd.tex}
  \end{center}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 4: weight sweep}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{plots/lambda_sweep.pdf}
  \end{center}
  \res
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item $\lambda=0.1$: depth \up{$-7.4$ to $-11.5\%$} against the best reference on
          \textbf{all three} scenes, at $>$7$\sigma$ on each (3-seed means, pooled standard
          error). First term in this report to improve depth everywhere.
    \item $\lambda=1$: more depth on \code{lone-monk} ($-12.9\%$), but \code{emerald-square}
          depth goes \dn{positive} and PSNR costs \dn{2.0\,dB}.
    \item $\lambda=10$: most of the depth gain given up; $\lambda=100$ diverges.
    \item Normals unchanged at every weight --- expected, since the rendered normal is the
          particle's local $z$ axis and depth ordering does not reach it.
  \end{itemize}
  \conc Usable band is narrow and centred on $\lambda=0.1$. Cost there: \up{$+0.12$\,dB} on
  \code{sponza}, \dn{$-0.20$} and \dn{$-0.63$\,dB} on the others.
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 4: qualitative}
  \qual \code{lone-monk} depth and relative error, against the reference and both reference runs.
  \begin{center}
    \quadrow
      {lone-monk/gt_f4_depth.png}{reference depth}
      {lone-monk/baseline_f4_depth.png}{\code{gaussian}}
      {lone-monk/trisurfel_f4_depth.png}{\code{trisurfel}}
      {lone-monk/pd01_f4_depth.png}{\code{pd 0.1}}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.2em}
  \begin{center}
    \panel{0.235}{lone-monk/baseline_f4_depth_err.png}{\code{gaussian} error}\hfill
    \panel{0.235}{lone-monk/trisurfel_f4_depth_err.png}{\code{trisurfel} error}\hfill
    \panel{0.235}{lone-monk/pd01_f4_depth_err.png}{\code{pd 0.1} error}\hfill
    \panel{0.235}{lone-monk/pd01_dn_f4_depth_err.png}{\code{pd 0.1 + dn} error}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.2em}
  \conc
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item The arch openings stay \dn{saturated} in every render: the ordinal term does
          \textbf{not} fix them.
    \item What improves is the diffuse error --- roof line, walls, ground all go blue.
    \item Consistent with the mechanism: pairs are drawn at $\le$5\% offsets and the prior is
          reliable locally (0.0116 per patch), not globally (0.0677). A hole in a wall is a
          long-range discontinuity.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\section{Experiment 5: the confidence gate}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 5: gating pairs by the prior's confidence}
  \begin{columns}[T]
    \begin{column}{0.46\textwidth}
      \pre Near-tied pairs are where the prior's sign is noise. Offline, on \code{sponza}:
      \begin{itemize}\small
        \item ordinal agreement with the reference, all pairs: 84\%
        \item after dropping pairs whose disparity gap is below 0.05 of the map's IQR:
              \textbf{97\%}
      \end{itemize}
      So ungated, roughly one pair in six pushes the wrong way.

      \expt Same term, same weight, gate on and off. 3 seeds each.
    \end{column}
    \begin{column}{0.52\textwidth}
      \begin{center}\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{plots/gate.pdf}\end{center}
    \end{column}
  \end{columns}
  \vspace{0.2em}
  \res
  \begin{center}\scriptsize
    \input{plots/tab_gate.tex}
  \end{center}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 5: conclusion}
  \res Neutral on \code{sponza} and \code{lone-monk} (within seed noise); on
  \code{emerald-square} it removes the entire gain, $-7.4\%$ becoming \dn{$+3.9\%$}.

  \conc \dn{Refuted.} Two reasons, both derivable from numbers already collected before the
  runs:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item A large disparity gap selects a \textbf{long-range} comparison --- precisely where
          this prior is weakest (0.0677 global against 0.0116 per patch). The gate keeps the
          prior's worst structure and discards its best.
    \item For a \textbf{one-sided} loss, 97\% agreement means only 3\% of surviving pairs can
          produce any gradient at all. High agreement is a warning, not a benefit.
  \end{itemize}
  The offline metric counted pairs instead of asking what they teach. Default is now off, pinned
  by a test so re-enabling it must be re-measured.
\end{frame}

\section{Experiment 6: combinations}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 6: combining terms}
  \pre The terms target different failures: internal consistency (\code{dn}, \code{dvrel})
  against an external prior (\code{pd}). Per the failure-mode table they should be
  complementary by scene.

  \expt Each term at its own measured optimum, and the pairs. Single seed.

  \res
  \begin{center}\scriptsize
    \input{plots/tab_combined.tex}
  \end{center}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 6: result}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth]{plots/compounding.pdf}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{-0.2em}
  \res
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item \textbf{Depth is sub-additive.} Pairs land near the \emph{max} of their parts, never
          the sum. On \code{lone-monk}, \code{pd + dn} ($-7.1\%$) is \dn{worse than \code{pd}
          alone} ($-10.8\%$).
    \item \textbf{Normals are super-additive.} \code{pd} alone does nothing for normals;
          \code{dn} alone leaves \code{lone-monk} below the control. \code{pd + dn} is the
          \textbf{only} configuration whose normals clear the control on all three scenes, and
          it beats \code{trisurfel} by 6.7--20.7$^\circ$.
    \item Mechanism: \code{dn} ties the normal to the depth \emph{gradient}, so it can only be
          as good as the depth given to it. The prior improves the depth; consistency carries
          that into normals.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 6: qualitative}
  \qual \code{lone-monk} normals. Same frame, same encoding.
  \begin{center}
    \quadrow
      {lone-monk/baseline_f4_normal_gt.png}{reference}
      {lone-monk/trisurfel_f4_normal.png}{\code{trisurfel} 35.0$^\circ$, \up{$+0.2$}}
      {lone-monk/dn05_f4_normal.png}{\code{dn 0.05} 37.4$^\circ$, \dn{$-2.1$}}
      {lone-monk/pd01_dn_f4_normal.png}{\code{pd + dn} \up{28.3$^\circ$}, \up{$+6.9$}}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.5em}
  \conc
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item \code{dn} alone: columns and arches blobby; still \dn{below the control}.
    \item \code{pd + dn}: colonnade resolved, and the only panel here whose \code{n\_gain} is
          meaningfully positive. Adding a depth term that touches no normals is what flipped the
          sign.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Experiment 6: the weight trap}
  \expt This pairing was first measured with $\lambda=1$ for \textbf{both} terms --- 10$\times$
  and 100$\times$ their measured optima --- and written up as a null.
  \res \code{abs\_rel}, and the change against each scene's best reference run.
  \begin{center}\scriptsize
    \input{plots/tab_trap.tex}
  \end{center}
  At their own optima the verdict changes from \emph{harmful} to \emph{scene-dependent}: the
  pair beats both single terms on \code{sponza}, is a wash on \code{lone-monk}, and is still
  worse than \code{pd} alone on \code{emerald-square}.

  \conc A null from a combination measured at the wrong weights is not a null about the
  combination. The over-weighted cell is kept in the sweep so the trap stays visible.
\end{frame}

\section{The photometric cost}

\begin{frame}{The photometric cost, localised}
  \expt PSNR is one number per frame and does not say where a difference sits. Difference every
  render against the reference image; same colour cap (10\% of full range) on every map.
  \begin{center}
    \panel{0.235}{emerald-square/gt_f4_rgb.png}{reference RGB}\hfill
    \panel{0.235}{emerald-square/baseline_f4_rgb_err.png}{\code{gaussian} 32.90\,dB}\hfill
    \panel{0.235}{emerald-square/trisurfel_f4_rgb_err.png}{\code{trisurfel} 32.92\,dB}\hfill
    \panel{0.235}{emerald-square/pd01_dn_f4_rgb_err.png}{\code{pd + dn} \dn{31.96\,dB}}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.4em}
  \res
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item Error in all three is concentrated in \textbf{foliage and the hedge line}; the road,
          buildings and sky are near zero everywhere.
    \item \code{pd + dn} replaces the references' fine speckle with \dn{larger coherent blobs}
          in the canopy: mean absolute RGB error 4.28 $\to$ \dn{4.80} of 255, closer to the
          reference on only \dn{41\%} of pixels.
  \end{itemize}
  \conc The cost is a real regression, not a metric artefact, and it is spatially specific ---
  vegetation, where a consistency term assuming a locally planar surface should be expected to
  pay most.
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The photometric cost, zoomed}
  \qual Canopy crop of the same frame, against the better reference run here by PSNR.
  \code{gaussian} carries the same artifacts and is omitted for space.
  \begin{center}
    % The band with the largest error increase, located from the difference maps rather than by
    % eye: x in [0,240], y in [60,240] of the 640x360 frame.
    \panelcrop{0.31}{0 120 400 60}{emerald-square/gt_f4_rgb.png}{reference}\hfill
    \panelcrop{0.31}{0 120 400 60}{emerald-square/trisurfel_f4_rgb.png}{\code{trisurfel} 32.92\,dB}\hfill
    \panelcrop{0.31}{0 120 400 60}{emerald-square/pd01_dn_f4_rgb.png}{\code{pd + dn} \dn{31.97\,dB}}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.2em}
  \res Two changes at once:
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item The references' \textbf{spiky starburst artifacts} (left of frame) are \up{gone} ---
          they are not in the reference image either.
    \item Genuine foliage structure is \dn{smoothed away} with them, and against the reference
          that costs more than the artifacts did.
  \end{itemize}
  \conc Removing visible artifacts and losing PSNR are not contradictory, but here the loss is
  not paid for: the render moves away from the reference on the majority of pixels.
\end{frame}

\section{Summary}

\begin{frame}{Summary: depth}
  \res \code{abs\_rel}, and the change against each scene's \textbf{best reference run}.
  \begin{center}\scriptsize
    \input{plots/tab_depth_summary.tex}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.5em}
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item \code{pd 0.1} is the only \emph{single} term improving depth on all three scenes by
          more than seed noise ($\pm$0.002--0.004). \code{dn 0.05}'s \code{lone-monk} and
          \code{emerald-square} gains (0.0005, 0.0018) are inside it; \code{dvrel} loses on
          \code{lone-monk}. Both pairs clear it on all three, at single seed.
    \item Best per scene: \code{pd + dn} on \code{sponza}, \code{pd} alone on \code{lone-monk}
          and \code{emerald-square}.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Summary: normals}
  \res Mean angle, and the change against each scene's \textbf{best reference run} (which is
  \code{trisurfel} on all three).
  \begin{center}\scriptsize
    \input{plots/tab_normal_summary.tex}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.5em}
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item \code{pd} and \code{dvrel} leave normals unchanged; both act on depth only.
    \item \code{pd + dn} is best on all three scenes, and the only configuration with positive
          \code{n\_gain} everywhere.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Status and settings}
  \begin{center}\small
  \begin{tabular}{lll}
    \toprule
    Term & Status & Verdict \\
    \midrule
    Depth--normal consistency & \up{landed}, off & Recovers normals; \code{lone-monk} still loses to \code{trisurfel} \\
    Depth variance, absolute & \dn{refuted} & Confidence without accuracy; \code{wrong\,|\,tight} $\times$170 \\
    Depth variance, relative & \up{landed}, off & Depth on \code{sponza} only; null elsewhere, no cost \\
    Scale-$z$ (PGSR port) & \up{landed}, small & Only after fixing the normal-axis assumption \\
    Pseudo-depth regression & \dn{abandoned} & Prior worse than the model it would teach \\
    Pseudo-depth ordinal & \up{landed}, off & Only single term improving depth on all 3 scenes \\
    \quad + confidence gate & \dn{refuted} & Keeps the prior's worst structure \\
    Multi-view consistency, mesh & not started & \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{0.6em}
  \begin{itemize}\small
    \item Depth, one term: \code{pd 0.1}. $-7$ to $-11\%$ against the best reference on all
          three scenes, $+0.12$ to $-0.63$\,dB.
    \item Depth and normals: \code{pd 0.1 + dn 0.05}. Best normals everywhere, $-0.22$ to $-0.95$\,dB.
    \item All remain \textbf{off by default}: the photometric cost is real and PSNR is what the
          codebase is currently evaluated on.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Limitations}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{7k iterations only.} No term confirmed at 30k. Iteration-gated defaults
          (\code{*\_from\_iter}) were lowered for the sweep and do not transfer unchanged.
    \item \textbf{Three scenes}, chosen because they fail differently, not because they are
          representative.
    \item \textbf{Combination cells are single-seed} against 3-seed references. The
          \code{lone-monk} \code{n\_gain} sign flip and the \code{sponza} depth gains are far
          outside seed noise; \code{emerald-square} differences of $\sim$1 point are not.
    \item \textbf{Why \code{emerald-square} pays most is unexplained.} That the cost is
          concentrated in foliage is measured; the link to its depth range is a hypothesis.
    \item \textbf{No mesh.} Nothing here is evaluated by surface extraction or Chamfer distance.
    \item \textbf{The prior diagnostic is \code{sponza}-only}, and \code{DepthAnythingV2-Base}
          only.
  \end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Method notes that changed a conclusion}
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Include a control that uses no information.} \code{gaussian}'s normal buffer
          looked reasonable and lost to pointing every normal at the camera;
          \code{trisurfel}'s looks good, scores 19$^\circ$ better, and still only ties the
          control.
    \item \textbf{Report per scene.} \code{lone-monk} has no floaters and the worst depth; a
          whole family of terms cannot help it, and a scene mean reported a win.
    \item \textbf{Compare against the strongest reference, not the one you modified.} Every
          treatment here is a change to \code{gaussian}, so \code{gaussian} was the natural
          baseline --- but \code{trisurfel} is better on normals everywhere and on
          \code{emerald-square} depth. Re-scoring against the best of the two removed a claim
          that \code{dn 0.05} beat all references on normals, and cut \code{pd 0.1}'s
          \code{emerald-square} depth gain from 10.3\% to 7.4\%.
    \item \textbf{Measure the reference quantity before building on it.} The prior diagnostic
          cancelled a planned loss; the PGSR port regressed normals 30$^\circ$ because
          ``min scale'' is not this renderer's normal axis.
    \item \textbf{An offline metric can motivate the wrong mechanism.} The gate's
          84\%$\to$97\% was real and irrelevant.
    \item \textbf{Measure combinations at each term's own optimum}, and against each single
          term, not only against a baseline.
    \item \textbf{Localise a metric before interpreting it.} The RGB difference maps turned an
          assumed metric artefact into a measured regression.
  \end{enumerate}
\end{frame}
